# Informed Consent Form: Study J1I-MC-GZQO (synthetic, version 2.0)

This consent form is fictional. It was written for TrialBox testing and is not the sponsor's or any hospital's consent form.

## 1. Why is this study being done?

You are being asked to take part in a research study because you have gout and a body mass index of 27 or higher. The study is testing a medicine called retatrutide. Retatrutide is an investigational medicine, which means it is not approved for sale in Taiwan or any other country.

The purpose of the study is to find out whether retatrutide, given once a week, lowers the level of uric acid in the blood and reduces gout flares compared with placebo. A placebo is an injection that looks like the study medicine but contains no medicine.

About 900 people at about 120 hospitals in 10 countries will take part. About 30 people will take part at this hospital.

## 2. What will happen if I take part?

The study has a screening period of up to 4 weeks and a treatment period of 52 weeks, followed by a safety follow-up visit 4 weeks after your last dose. In total you will be in the study for about 60 weeks.

You will be assigned by chance, like rolling a die, to one of three groups: retatrutide 4 mg, retatrutide 8 mg, or placebo. You have a 1 in 3 chance of receiving placebo. Neither you nor the study doctor will know which group you are in.

You will inject the study medicine under the skin of your belly or thigh once a week, on the same day each week. The study staff will teach you how to give the injection.

You will come to the hospital for 14 visits. Most visits take about 2 hours. At the visits the study staff will take blood samples (about 2 tablespoons each time), measure your weight and blood pressure, and ask about your health and your medicines.

You must keep taking your usual gout medicine that lowers uric acid during the study, unless the study doctor tells you otherwise.

## 3. What are the possible risks and discomforts?

The most common side effects seen with medicines like retatrutide are nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and constipation. In earlier studies, nausea happened in about 4 out of 10 people. These effects were usually mild to moderate and happened most often when the dose was increased.

Retatrutide may cause inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis), which can be serious. Stop the injections and call the study doctor right away if you have severe stomach pain that does not go away, with or without vomiting.

In studies in rodents, medicines like retatrutide caused thyroid tumors. It is not known whether this happens in people. You cannot take part if you or a family member has had medullary thyroid cancer.

You may get a gout flare when your uric acid level changes. The study doctor will give you medicine to treat flares.

Blood draws may cause pain, bruising or, rarely, fainting or infection where the needle goes in.

Retatrutide may harm an unborn baby. If you can become pregnant, you must use an effective method of birth control during the study and for 2 months after your last dose. Tell the study doctor at once if you become pregnant.

There may be risks that are not known yet.

## 4. Are there benefits to taking part?

You may or may not benefit from taking part in this study. Your uric acid level, gout flares or weight may improve, but this cannot be promised. What we learn may help other people with gout in the future.

## 5. What other choices do I have?

You do not have to take part in this study to receive treatment for gout. Other choices include your current gout medicines, other approved medicines that lower uric acid, and advice about diet and weight. Your doctor can talk with you about these choices.

## 6. What will I need to do?

You will need to come to all study visits, inject the study medicine every week, and write down any side effects and gout flares in the study diary. You must not take part in any other research study involving a medicine at the same time. Do not start any weight-loss medicine during the study.

## 7. Is taking part voluntary?

Taking part is voluntary. You can decide not to take part, or you can stop at any time, without giving a reason. If you decide not to take part or to stop, you will not lose any benefits or medical care you would otherwise get at this hospital. If you stop, the study doctor will ask you to come for a final safety visit.

## 8. How will my information be protected?

Your study records will be labelled with a code number, not your name. Only the study team, the ethics committee, the sponsor's monitors and health authorities may look at your medical records to check the study. Your name will not appear in any report or publication.

## 9. Costs, payments and injury

The study medicine and study tests are free. You will receive NT$1,000 for each completed visit to cover travel costs. If you are injured because of taking part in this study, the sponsor will pay for the medical care you need, as described in the injury section of the full form.

## 10. Who can I contact?

If you have questions about the study or a side effect, call the study coordinator, Ms. Lin, at 02-2312-3456 extension 7701, Monday to Friday, 9:00 to 17:00. After hours, call the hospital emergency line at 02-2312-3456 extension 9.

If you have questions about your rights as a research participant, call the Research Ethics Committee at 02-2312-3456 extension 5200.

## 11. Signature

Signing the official consent form means that you have read it or had it read to you, that your questions have been answered, and that you agree to take part. You will receive a signed copy.
